title: 1 Samuel 10:1–16
context: Samuel anoints Saul privately with oil as prince over the LORD’s inheritance and gives him three signs to confirm the word: two men at Rachel’s tomb will report the donkeys found, three men going up to God at Bethel will give him bread, and at the hill of God a band of prophets will meet him, when the LORD’s Spirit will come mightily on him and he will prophesy and be turned into another man. Saul is told to go to Gilgal and wait seven days for Samuel. As he leaves, God gives him another heart, the signs come to pass, and he prophesies, giving rise to the proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” Saul tells his uncle only about the donkeys. Both traditions agree God truly equips Saul for his office; they differ mainly in how they relate that equipping to the deeper renewal of the heart.

verses.text: Then Samuel took the vial of oil and poured it on his head, then kissed him and said, “Hasn’t the LORD anointed you to be prince over his inheritance?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the anointing comes with a question that presses the truth home: hasn’t the LORD anointed you? Saul is set apart by God for real service over the LORD’s inheritance, and the honor carries a corresponding responsibility to rule as God’s servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that Saul is anointed prince over “his inheritance,” that is, the LORD’s own people. The king is a steward under the true King, and the anointing marks God’s appointment to office rather than any claim Saul has to the throne in his own right.

verses.text: When you have departed from me today, then you will find two men by Rachel’s tomb, on the border of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will tell you, ‘The donkeys which you went to look for have been found; and behold, your father has stopped caring about the donkeys and is anxious for you, saying, “What shall I do for my son?” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the first sign, two men by Rachel’s tomb reporting the donkeys found, as God’s kindness in confirming his word in ways Saul can recognize. God gives evidence that invites trust rather than demanding belief without support.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the precise foretelling of the two men’s words confirms that Samuel speaks God’s word. The location of Rachel’s tomb here, on Benjamin’s border at Zelzah, raises a geographical question in relation to Genesis 35:19, and the exact site of Zelzah is uncertain.

verses.text: “Then you will go on forward from there, and you will come to the oak of Tabor. Three men will meet you there going up to God to Bethel: one carrying three young goats, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a container of wine.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the second sign: three men going up to God at Bethel, carrying goats, bread, and wine. The specific details are meant to build Saul’s confidence that the anointing is real and that God is guiding him step by step.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the detailed prediction about men going up to worship at Bethel displays God’s foreknowledge of ordinary human movements. The exact location of the oak of Tabor is unknown, but the sign’s function as confirmation is clear.

verses.text: They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall receive from their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Saul is to receive two loaves from these worshipers. The gift is a small token of the provision and honor that will attend his new role, and receiving it is part of Saul’s willing participation in the signs God has given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gift of bread from worshipers bound for Bethel as a quiet sign that Saul is being received as one set apart. Some interpreters see an anticipation of the tribute due a king, though the text itself does not explain the gesture.

verses.text: “After that you will come to the hill of God, where the garrison of the Philistines is; and it will happen, when you have come there to the city, that you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the high place with a lute, a tambourine, a pipe, and a harp before them; and they will be prophesying.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the third sign will take place at the hill of God near a Philistine garrison, with a band of prophets prophesying to music. The setting reminds Saul of the very threat he has been called to address and shows God meeting him in the midst of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the presence of a Philistine garrison at the hill of God, probably near Gibeah though the identification is uncertain, sets the national need beside the divine provision. Saul is being prepared for the deliverance the LORD promised in 9:16.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s Spirit will come mightily on you, then you will prophesy with them and will be turned into another man.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers read the LORD’s Spirit coming mightily on Saul as a genuine empowering for the task God has given him. Being turned into another man describes a real transformation suited to his calling, which Saul is then responsible to steward faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a real work of the Spirit that equips Saul for kingship, comparable to the Spirit coming on the judges (Judges 14:6). Many Reformed interpreters distinguish this empowering for office from regenerating grace, while acknowledging that the text does not spell out the inner effects.

verses.text: Let it be, when these signs have come to you, that you do what is appropriate for the occasion; for God is with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the instruction that once the signs come, Saul should do what is appropriate for the occasion, because God is with him. God’s presence does not replace Saul’s initiative but calls him to act with courage and wisdom in the opportunities that arise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the assurance “God is with you” is the foundation of Saul’s commission. The signs confirm God’s word, and the call to act fittingly rests on God’s presence rather than on Saul’s natural qualities, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: “Go down ahead of me to Gilgal; and behold, I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice sacrifices of peace offerings. Wait seven days, until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the command to go to Gilgal and wait seven days for Samuel. This becomes a test of obedience that Saul will later fail (1 Samuel 13:8–14), showing that the gift of the Spirit and the anointing do not remove the need for faithful, patient obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the seven-day instruction as preparing the test of 1 Samuel 13:8–14. The king remains under the prophetic word: Saul must wait for God’s messenger and God’s instruction, and his later impatience will reveal his failure to submit to that order.

verses.text: It was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart; and all those signs happened that day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers understand God giving Saul “another heart” as a genuine inner change that equipped him for kingship and opened a real path of faithfulness. Because Saul later turns from that path, many Arminians see the account as showing that God’s gifts can be truly given and yet neglected or resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God truly changed Saul as he turned to go, but many read “another heart” as a renewal of disposition and courage for office rather than the new heart of regeneration. On this reading, Saul’s later rejection fits with the view that office-gifts can be withdrawn while saving grace endures. Both traditions affirm that God really changed Saul for his calling, and neither speaks with one voice on Saul’s spiritual state.

verses.text: When they came there to the hill, behold, a band of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came mightily on him, and he prophesied among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Spirit of God comes mightily on Saul exactly as foretold, and he prophesies among the prophets. The fulfillment confirms God’s faithfulness to his word and shows Saul genuinely caught up in what God is doing at this moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the fulfillment of the sign confirms Samuel’s word and God’s choice of Saul. The Spirit’s coming here is an outward, visible empowering, and both traditions recognize that in the Old Testament the Spirit often comes upon leaders to equip them for particular tasks.

verses.text: When all who knew him before saw that, behold, he prophesied with the prophets, then the people said to one another, “What is this that has come to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the astonishment of those who knew Saul before: what has come to the son of Kish? The change in Saul is visible and surprising, testifying that God’s work in a person can be real and public, even before its long-term fruit is known.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the bystanders’ surprise as evidence that the change is God’s doing rather than Saul’s natural development. The question also leaves room for ambiguity, since later in the story the same saying will return in a darker setting (1 Samuel 19:24).

verses.text: One from the same place answered, “Who is their father?” Therefore it became a proverb, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the reply “Who is their father?” is hard to interpret; it may question the prophets’ lineage or suggest that prophetic gifts come from God rather than family. The proverb that results shows how memorable and unexpected Saul’s experience was.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge that “Who is their father?” is obscure; it may imply that prophecy depends on God’s gift rather than on human descent. The proverb captures the surprise of Saul’s experience, and interpreters in both traditions hold their readings of it tentatively.

verses.text: When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that when the prophesying ends, Saul goes to the high place. The ecstatic moment passes, and ordinary life resumes, which reminds readers that a vivid experience of God’s Spirit must be followed by steady faithfulness in daily obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the prophesying is a temporary sign rather than a lasting office for Saul. He returns to the high place, and the narrative moves on, keeping the focus on God’s appointment of Saul as king rather than on the experience itself.

verses.text: Saul’s uncle said to him and to his servant, “Where did you go?” He said, “To seek the donkeys. When we saw that they were not found, we came to Samuel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Saul’s brief answer to his uncle about seeking the donkeys and coming to Samuel. He tells the truth but not the whole story, and the narrative leaves readers to wonder whether this reflects modesty, caution, or uncertainty about his new calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s reply is accurate as far as it goes. Whether his reticence reflects humility or hesitation is not stated, and readers in both traditions differ; the story simply records that the anointing remained private for now.

verses.text: Saul’s uncle said, “Please tell me what Samuel said to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the uncle’s request to hear what Samuel said as natural curiosity within the family. The question gives Saul an opportunity to speak of what God has done, and his response will show how he chooses to handle that opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the uncle presses for Samuel’s words, recognizing the prophet’s significance. The narrative uses the exchange to keep the anointing hidden until God’s appointed public choice at Mizpah in the following passage.

verses.text: Saul said to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the donkeys were found.” But concerning the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel spoke, he didn’t tell him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Saul tells his uncle the donkeys were found but says nothing about the kingdom. His silence may be prudent or reluctant, and either way the public recognition of his calling is left for the assembly that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul keeps the matter of the kingdom to himself. Whatever his motive, the silence allows the LORD to reveal his choice publicly through the lot at Mizpah, so that Israel will see the king as the one “whom the LORD has chosen” (10:24).
